pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Collect and describe different samples of soils, such as sandy soil, loamy soil and clay soil, from the school garden and the community.
- Discuss how each soil type retains water and supports the root system of plants.
- Conduct an experiment to demonstrate how different soil types retain water to support the root system of crops.

pages.title: What Determines a Soil's Physical Properties?
pages.body: Particle size, texture, and the proportion of sand, silt and clay present are the main factors that determine the physical properties of a soil, which in turn affect how well that soil retains water and supports plant growth. Sandy soil, loamy soil and clay soil are three common soil types studied at this level, each with distinctly different physical properties.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Comparing Sandy, Loamy and Clay Soil

pages.title: Comparing Sandy, Loamy and Clay Soil
pages.body:
Particle size, water retention, and support for plant roots are three key physical properties used to compare sandy soil, loamy soil and clay soil, as summarised in the table below.

| **SOIL TYPE** | **PARTICLE SIZE** | **WATER RETENTION** | **SUPPORT FOR ROOTS** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sandy soil** | Large particles, feels gritty | Poor, water drains quickly | Loose, offers limited support and nutrients |
| **Loamy soil** | A balanced mix of sand, silt and clay | Good, retains enough water without waterlogging | Excellent, supports strong root growth |
| **Clay soil** | Very fine particles, feels sticky when wet | Very high, can become waterlogged | Compact, can restrict root growth if too dense |

pages.title: How Soil Type Affects Water Retention and Root Support
pages.body: Pore space between particles, and how tightly those particles pack together, are what mainly determine how much water a soil can hold and how easily roots can grow through it. Sandy soil has large pore spaces that let water pass through quickly, meaning plants grown in sandy soil often need more frequent watering. Clay soil has very small pore spaces that hold water tightly, which can support water availability but may also lead to waterlogging and poor root aeration if not managed carefully. Loamy soil balances these properties, generally making it the preferred soil type for most crop production.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Investigating Water Retention in Different Soils

pages.title: Investigating Water Retention in Different Soils
pages.body: Collecting soil samples, applying an equal amount of water to each, and measuring how much water drains through or is retained are the general steps of a simple experiment that can demonstrate how different soil types retain water. Comparing the time taken for water to drain through each sample, and the amount of water left in each sample afterwards, provides clear, direct evidence of the differences in water retention between sandy, loamy and clay soil.

pages.title: More Physical Properties of Sandy, Loamy and Clay Soils
pages.body:
| **PROPERTY** | **SANDY SOIL** | **LOAMY SOIL** | **CLAY SOIL** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Size of particles** | Largest, about 0.05 to 2 millimetres | A mixture of sand, silt and clay | Smallest, less than 0.002 millimetres |
| **Feel** | Gritty and loose | Soft and crumbly | Smooth and sticky when wet, hard when dry |
| **Air spaces** | Large, so it is well aerated | Moderate | Very small, so it is poorly aerated |
| **Drainage** | Very fast | Moderate | Very slow, so it is easily waterlogged |
| **Water holding capacity** | Low | Good | High |
| **Capillarity** | Water rises only a short distance | Water rises a moderate distance | Water rises highest, but slowly |
| **Nutrients and humus** | Few, because they are washed out | Rich | Rich in minerals but hard for roots to reach |
| **Ease of working** | Light and easy to dig | Easy to dig | Heavy and hard to dig |

Silt particles are between sand and clay in size and feel smooth like flour. Capillarity is the rise of water through the tiny spaces between soil particles, in the way that kerosene rises up the wick of a lantern. It brings water from deeper in the soil up to the roots during dry weather.

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:ibde8c2f1b|Fig 9.1  Comparing the particle arrangement of sandy, loamy and clay soil]]

Notice how sandy soil has large, widely spaced particles that allow water to drain through quickly, while clay soil has very fine, tightly packed particles that hold water strongly but drain slowly. Loamy soil, with its balanced mix of particle sizes, tends to offer the best combination of water retention and drainage for most crops.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Farmers often improve soil physical properties by adding organic matter, such as compost or well rotted manure, which can help sandy soil retain more water and help clay soil drain more freely, moving both soil types closer to the balanced properties of loamy soil. This practical knowledge of soil properties directly supports better decision making in crop production, which is explored further in the next lesson.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Soil Water Content and Importance in Crop Production

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Examine and discuss the different physical properties of each soil type and how these properties help support crop production.
- Observe and describe the growth of different plants on different soil types.
- Demonstrate how plants absorb water and nutrients from the soil (osmosis).

pages.title: Why Soil Water Content Matters for Crop Production
pages.body: Soil water content refers to the amount of water held within the spaces between soil particles at any given time, and it directly affects how well crops can grow in that soil. Too little water content leaves plants unable to absorb enough water for their life processes, causing wilting and poor growth, while too much water content can starve plant roots of oxygen and encourage root diseases. Matching a crop to a soil with an appropriate water content is therefore an important part of successful crop production.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Matching Crops to Suitable Soil Types

pages.title: Matching Crops to Suitable Soil Types
pages.body:
Sandy soil, loamy soil and clay soil each suit different crops, depending on how well that crop tolerates or benefits from the particular water retention properties of the soil, as summarised in the table below.

| **SOIL TYPE** | **SUITABLE CROPS** | **REASON FOR SUITABILITY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Sandy soil** | Carrots, groundnut, cassava | These crops develop underground and benefit from loose soil that is easy to expand into, and tolerate lower water retention |
| **Loamy soil** | Maize, tomato, most vegetables | The balanced water retention and nutrient availability support strong, healthy growth for a wide range of crops |
| **Clay soil** | Rice, some leafy vegetables | These crops tolerate or even benefit from consistently moist, water retentive soil conditions |

pages.title: How Plants Absorb Water and Nutrients, Osmosis
pages.body:
Osmosis is the movement of water from an area where it is more concentrated, such as moist soil, into an area where it is less concentrated, such as inside a plant root cell, passing through a thin, selectively permeable membrane. Root hairs, tiny extensions on plant roots, greatly increase the surface area available for this water uptake. Once inside the root, water and dissolved nutrients move upward through the stem to reach the leaves, flowers and fruits, supporting the plant's overall growth and development.

10.4  Practical Illustration

[[img:i4a19d9e38|]]

Fig 10.1  How plant roots absorb water and nutrients from soil through osmosis, and transport them upward through the stem

Notice how water moves from the soil, where it is generally more concentrated, into the root hairs, and then continues moving upward through the stem, illustrating the complete pathway by which soil water content ultimately supports the whole plant, not just the roots.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Soil Water Content and Importance in Crop Production (part 3)

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:ibde8c2f1b|Fig 9.1  Different soil types support different crops based on their water retention and structural properties]]

Notice that root and tuber crops such as cassava generally do well in looser, sandy soils that allow easy expansion underground, while water loving crops such as rice thrive in the moisture retentive conditions of clay soil. Observing and recording how the same crop grows differently when planted in different soil types can provide direct evidence of these relationships.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Farmers can use simple field observations, such as how quickly water disappears after rainfall or irrigation, to estimate their soil's water retention properties without needing laboratory equipment. Combining this practical knowledge of soil water content with an understanding of which crops suit which soil types allows farmers to make more informed decisions when selecting crops or improving their land for future planting seasons.
